title: Drinking Water Operations and Regulatory Compliance
audience: Drinking-water operators, supervisors and records reviewers in the United States and Canada who prepare, review or hand over operational evidence after a drinking-water event. The course is jurisdiction-neutral: the applicable regulator, permit or licence sets every requirement, limit, interval and recipient for a given system. This course teaches you to find those sources, check their applicability and keep the evidence separate from the conclusions. It does not confer an operator designation.
prerequisites: Working familiarity with a drinking-water treatment or distribution system and basic operational records. Familiarity with your own jurisdiction's drinking-water regulator is helpful. This course does not confer an operator designation.
introduction: Build an auditable response to a changing drinking-water event. Working from a supplied fictional document register, sampling records, laboratory messages and a shift log, you will map each decision to its governing source and the person responsible, reconcile conflicting records, separate reporting from corrective action and closure, correct records without losing the original observation, and defend a handover. The course is jurisdiction-neutral. Ontario appears only as one labelled worked example, and the Ontario sources are named as an example of how to check a requirement, not as the rule for your system. Sample identity and holding-time arithmetic are taught in ceu-sampling-data-quality. Treatment monitoring, CT and T10 are taught in ceu-water-treatment-process-control and ceu-coagulation-filtration. Those topics are used here only where the compliance decision depends on them.
delivery: Self-paced lessons, six graded checks per module, a graded final exam and an alternate final exam. Planned time is 360 minutes, 60 minutes per module. This is a non-credit pilot; duration is being validated and no contact-hour award is made.

modules.title: Build the compliance and responsibility map
objectives: Distinguish a legal requirement, a system authorization, a controlled procedure and an observation.
Assign a case task to a verified role and identify unresolved authority.
Create a source register that another operator can independently check.
modules.lesson: ### Start with the decision, not the document This is study and training material for a non-credit pilot. It is not operating or compliance instruction. Facilities, people, records and readings are fictional, and example quantities are supplied case assumptions, not authorized values. The applicable regulator, permit or licence sets the rules for a real system. Those rules differ between US states, Canadian provinces and territories, and individual systems. Every requirement in this course is therefore attributed to a source you must check. Ontario appears only as one labelled worked example. A compliance map connects a decision to the source that governs it, the person responsible and the evidence that the required action occurred. "Who handles compliance?" is too broad to check. "Which verified role held responsibility for the affected process during the event, and what record shows that?" can be answered and verified. Record the system, the activity, the event date, the treatment configuration and the version of each document you rely on. Separate documents in force when the event occurred from documents in force today. A current designation does not show who held a role during an earlier event. ### Classify each item before you rely on it - **Legal requirement:** a statute or regulation that establishes a duty. - **System authorization:** a permit or licence that sets conditions or permissions for one system. - **Controlled procedure:** an approved method for carrying out work within those requirements. - **Observation:** a measurement, record, communication or action. An observation does not create authority. A checklist cannot authorize a configuration the permit does not cover. A procedure cannot remove a statutory duty. When two documents conflict, record the conflict and route it for authorized interpretation. Do not choose the easier instruction. ### Build a source register another person can check A register gives a retrieval path, not just a bibliography. Record the exact title, the issuing body, the provision, the version or effective date, the controlled location, the applicability and any linked performance evidence. Enter "not verified" where a detail is unavailable. | Decision to support | Source to check | Applicability question | Evidence of performance | |---|---|---|---| | Who held overall responsibility? | Operator designation rules (US: state certification rules; Canada: provincial or territorial regulation; Ontario example: O. Reg. 128/04) | Does the designation cover this system and date? | Designation, scope and qualification record | | Who was responsible for the process? | Designation and duty provisions, plus the facility assignment procedure | Does the assignment cover this process and period? | Operator-in-charge assignment and operating records | | What reporting applies to an adverse result? | US: 40 CFR Part 141 and state rules; Ontario example: SDWA s. 18 and O. Reg. 170/03, Schedule 16 | What result, duty holder, recipients and exemptions apply? | Notice, call and transmission records | | Which system conditions govern? | The system's permit or licence | Right system, configuration and version? | Controlled condition reference | | Can a turbidity trend support the account? | US EPA, EPA 815-B-19-010 (technical guidance) | Is the measurement chain understood? | Instrument status and maintenance records | The EPA document can inform scrutiny of measurement quality. It cannot establish a reporting trigger or replace a system's permit. Keep authority and performance in separate fields. A regulation shows that a duty exists. A transmission record shows that a notice was sent. Neither substitutes for the other. ### Match the task to a documented role A task is assigned only when a current record shows which role owns it for the process and period. Start with the record, not the familiar name. 1. **Name the task** specifically. 2. **Check the role record**: role, process scope and effective period. 3. **Confirm the person** and how the handover was recorded. A supervisor's title does not prove a designation. An operator certificate supports qualification, not an assignment. A contact list shows how to reach someone, not who holds decision authority. If the record is unclear, write "authority not confirmed" and route the question through the controlled procedure. ### Worked example: a period not supported by assignment records The review period runs from 06:00 to 18:00. A verified record covers Amira as operator-in-charge of the affected process from 06:00 to 12:00. Another covers Lee from 14:00 to 18:00. A relief binder says "Morgan covers lunch," but gives no effective date, scope or designation basis. Step 1. Review duration = 18 h − 6 h = 12 h. Step 2. Amira's supported interval = 12 h − 6 h = 6 h. Step 3. Lee's supported interval = 18 h − 14 h = 4 h. Step 4. The intervals do not overlap, so the supported total = 6 h + 4 h = 10 h. Step 5. Unsupported interval = 12 h − 10 h = 2 h, from 12:00 to 14:00. **Answer:** the verified records support 10 h of the 12 h period. The remaining 2 h is an evidence gap, not proof that nobody qualified was present. An event at 13:10 falls in that gap, so Morgan cannot be assigned responsibility from the binder alone. If a verified record later covers the gap, revise the finding and keep the original review visible. ### Worked example: a reporting timeline with a labelled assumption **Classroom assumption, for arithmetic only and not a rule:** written notice is due within 24 hours after the verbal report. The applicable regulation or permit sets the real interval, recipients and content. For the Ontario example, the sources are section 18 of the Safe Drinking Water Act, 2002 and Schedule 16 of Ontario Regulation 170/03. Verbal report: 08:20 on 12 November. Written submission: 07:05 on 13 November. Both use the same local time basis. Step 1. Verbal report = (8 × 60) + 20 = 500 min after midnight on 12 November. Step 2. Written submission = (7 × 60) + 5 = 425 min after midnight on 13 November. Step 3. Elapsed time = (1,440 − 500) + 425 = 1,365 min = 22.75 h. Step 4. Remaining in the classroom window = 1,440 − 1,365 = 75 min. **Answer:** on the classroom assumption, written submission occurred 22.75 h after the verbal report, with 75 minutes to spare. This supports the timing only. It does not show that the recipients, the content or the other duties were met. A draft saved before transmission proves preparation, not submission. ### Common errors - **Treating a binder as authority.** A binder can hold current and obsolete material together. - **Equating seniority with designation.** Rank does not prove the role, the scope or the period. - **Adding overlapping intervals.** This counts the same time twice and can hide a gap. - **Using a draft's creation time as the submission time.** - **Treating technical guidance as binding law** for your system. ### Verify before you act Before a responsibility finding, check the designation provisions that apply, the designation and assignment records and their effective dates. Before a reporting finding, check the current reporting provisions for your system: 40 CFR Part 141 and state rules in the United States, the provincial or territorial regulation in Canada, and, for the Ontario example, section 18 of the Safe Drinking Water Act, 2002 and Schedule 16 of Ontario Regulation 170/03. Check the facility's reporting procedure, the recipients and any claimed exemption. Before a treatment finding, consult the permit or licence and the approved calculation basis. A reviewer should be able to reproduce the arithmetic and retrieve the same source versions without asking the author. The handover should state what is established, what is unsupported and the route for each open issue, without inventing a deadline or a replacement authority.
modules.evidence:
### Fictional worked scenario: reporting evidence and unresolved authority

The facility, operators, records and readings in this scenario are fictional. All case times are supplied teaching assumptions, not authorized values. This is a non-credit training exercise.

At fictional Maple Crossing Drinking Water System, the supplied case records a reportable adverse laboratory result and a verbal report completed at 13:40 on 18 February 2026. The case uses the classroom assumption of a 24-hour written-notice window after the verbal report, and it supplies a transmission record for written notice to the required recipients at 12:55 on 19 February 2026. Both timestamps use the same time basis.

A spreadsheet lists 09:10 on 19 February as "report complete." Its only support is a locally saved draft. Reject 09:10 as evidence of submission. Retain it as evidence of preparation.

The current verified assignment names Amira as operator-in-charge for the affected process during the event. An undated binder names Morgan as "incident lead." The binder does not establish a designation or reporting authority. Amira's assignment supports the process-role finding but does not establish that all reporting duties belonged to Amira alone.

**Worked timing solution:**

Verbal report position = (13 × 60) + 40 = 820 min after midnight on 18 February.
Written submission position = (12 × 60) + 55 = 775 min after midnight on 19 February.
Elapsed time = (1,440 − 820) + 775 = 1,395 min = 23.25 h.
Remaining in the classroom window = 1,440 − 1,395 = 45 min.

**Answer:** the transmission record supports written submission within the classroom window, with 45 minutes remaining. The spreadsheet entry of 09:10 does not establish submission. Retain the laboratory notification, the verbal report record, the submitted notice, the transmission evidence and the verified assignment. Resolve Morgan's claimed authority separately, using the applicable designation rules rather than the binder.
modules.assignment: Prepare a four-row source register covering role designation, incident ownership, reporting applicability and record correction. Build a responsibility matrix for the shift. Identify two conflicts or missing pieces of evidence, name the task owner that the case supports, and state what you cannot conclude. Then write a 100-word handover that accepts or declines each open task, with a reason for each decision.
rubric: Links each proposed duty to a source category and a supplied record; does not treat a job title as a designation.
Identifies the undated binder as unsupported and names the missing evidence without inventing qualifications or alternate authority.
Assigns the open event to the role that the records support and gives a traceable handover or escalation path.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Expected matrix: the verified assignment supports Amira for the affected process during the event. Morgan coordinates incidents but is not established as overall responsible operator or operator-in-charge. Ask learners which record names the event-file owner, and accept only the answer the designation record supports. The undated binder needs correction through document control, not deletion from the evidence file. Ask learners to distinguish a source that proves a duty from a record that proves it was discharged. Return submissions that assign every duty to Morgan or invent qualifications. Accept different register layouts if source, applicability and evidence remain separate.

checks.prompt: In a fictional case, which item should be classified as a system authorization rather than a legal requirement, controlled procedure or observation?
choices: A permit or licence covering this system's configuration
A controlled procedure describing the sampling method used by the crew
An operator's retained log describing a completed sampling round
A regulation establishing a reporting duty for adverse results
checks.explanation: A permit or licence is a system-specific instrument that sets conditions and permissions for one system, so it is the authorization. The procedure option is a controlled procedure: it describes an approved way to work but does not grant system permissions. The log option is an observation, since it records a completed round and creates no authority. The regulation option is a legal requirement that applies across systems, not a system-specific authorization. Confirm the current version of any named instrument.

checks.prompt: In a fictional case, a learner cites US EPA document EPA 815-B-19-010 when reviewing turbidity records. What use of this source is appropriate?
choices: Use it to replace the system-specific conditions for turbidity monitoring
Use it to examine measurement quality while checking applicable duties
Use it to decide treatment permissions without consulting the permit
Use it to establish a reporting trigger for turbidity events
checks.explanation: EPA 815-B-19-010 is United States technical guidance on generating high-quality turbidity data. Its source page describes common turbidimeter setups, the SCADA systems that carry their data and best practices for data quality. It can inform scrutiny of instrument and SCADA evidence. The replacement option mistakes guidance for a permit condition. The permissions option ignores that treatment permissions come from the permit. The reporting option assumes guidance sets a trigger, which only the applicable regulation does.

checks.prompt: A fictional study file assigns an operator to prepare a notice. Which statement distinguishes task performance from legal responsibility?
choices: The reviewer becomes the sole duty holder once the draft has been checked
The owner keeps its duties only if the preparer asks for assistance
The assignment identifies a performer, not necessarily each duty holder
The preparer assumes every reporting duty as soon as drafting begins
checks.explanation: An assignment establishes who prepares a task. Which person or organization holds each legal duty is set by the applicable regulation or permit. The reviewer option assumes that checking a draft transfers duties. The owner option makes a duty depend on a request, which no regulation in this course supports. The preparer option assumes that drafting transfers every duty. Check duty holders against the applicable reporting provisions, for example 40 CFR Part 141 and state rules in the United States, or section 18 of the Safe Drinking Water Act, 2002 in the Ontario example.

checks.prompt: In a fictional case, a task message was sent to an alternate. The archive holds no delivery record, reply or action record. What does the supplied evidence establish?
choices: The alternate accepted responsibility when the message was sent
The task was completed, since the file contains no reply to report a problem
The alternate received the task through the designated contact route
The sender attempted communication, but receipt remains unverified
checks.explanation: A sent message establishes an attempt. It does not establish delivery, acceptance or action. The acceptance option treats dispatch as acceptance. The completion option treats the absence of a complaint as proof that work was done. The delivery option asserts receipt through a route that no delivery record shows.

checks.prompt: In a fictional case, the designation file contains no assignment covering the event period. Which finding stays within the available evidence?
choices: The file does not establish an effective assignment for the event period
The system necessarily breached each applicable designation requirement for the period
No qualified operator was present during the event under review
The assignment can be inferred from the most senior person listed
checks.explanation: The defensible finding is an evidence gap in the file. The breach option turns a missing record into a proven violation. The absence option claims more than the file can show, because a file cannot prove that nobody was present. The seniority option substitutes rank for designation. Designation rules are set by the applicable regulation; the Ontario example is O. Reg. 128/04, sections 23 and 25 to 27.

checks.prompt: In a fictional case, a source's title and issuer are known, but its relevant condition number is unavailable. How should the register represent that missing detail?
choices: Use the procedure paragraph number as the permit condition
Enter 'not verified' and identify the reference that needs confirmation
Copy a likely condition number from a comparable system's permit or approval
Leave the field empty and treat the document title as sufficient
checks.explanation: An explicit not verified entry keeps known and missing information separate and names the check that closes the gap. The procedure option uses another document's number as a permit condition. The comparable-system option borrows a condition from a system whose permit may differ. The empty-field option hides the gap, and a title does not identify a condition.

modules.title: Interpret control limits and conflicting measurements
objectives: Classify targets, alarms, action levels and requirements without conflating them.
Align observations by time, place, method and hydraulic context.
Bound missing evidence while keeping the protective response and the investigation separate.
modules.lesson: ### Four kinds of number, and why they must not be merged Operators work with four kinds of number every shift, and most bad interpretations come from treating one kind as another. A **target** is an internal operating preference. It keeps the process comfortably away from trouble. Missing a target is a process question, not a legal one. An **alarm** is an engineered notification in an instrument or control system. It fires on a configured value, deadband and delay. It proves only that the configured logic was satisfied by the signal that reached it. A silent panel does not prove compliance, because alarms can be suppressed, out of scan, in maintenance mode, or fed by a failed sensor. An **action level** is a trigger in a facility procedure that starts a specified response. It is usually set inside the requirement, so that response begins before the requirement is threatened. A **requirement** is a condition imposed by law or by the system's permit or licence. It has a defined scope: the parameter, the analyte form, the sampling point, the method, the averaging basis and the record that proves compliance. Two systems can carry different numbers for the same parameter because their permits differ. The numbers overlap, which is why the label matters. "Chlorine 0.55" means nothing until you know whether it is compared with a target, an alarm, an action level or a permit condition. ### Build the limit register before you read the trend A limit register ties every number you rely on to a source and a comparison rule. Build it before an event. Its value column is deliberately a pointer. The correct figure for your system is the one in your own permit, procedure or sampling plan, not one carried over from another facility. | Parameter | Units | Measurement point | Analyte form and method | Comparison rule | Governing document (fill in) | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Chlorine residual, treated water | mg/L | Clearwell outlet online analyzer | Free chlorine, method per procedure | Minimum value maintained | Permit or licence condition plus facility procedure | | Chlorine residual, distribution | mg/L | Named points in the sampling plan | Free and total, as specified | Value at time of sampling | Applicable regulation plus sampling plan | | Filter effluent turbidity | NTU | Each filter effluent | Nephelometric, continuous | Value and duration of exceedance | Permit plus facility procedure | | Internal residual warning (fictional) | mg/L | Same as online point | Free chlorine | Instantaneous | Facility target, no legal status | If an internal warning is not labelled as internal, someone will eventually report it as an exceedance, or argue that meeting it discharges a legal duty. The applicable regulation sets operator designation, duties and records. For the Ontario example, these are sections 23 and 25 to 27 of Ontario Regulation 128/04. ### Align observations: location, time, method, quality status When two measurements disagree, ask first whether they measure the same water. Run the four-point check in the figure below. **Location.** Is the grab tap upstream or downstream of the online point? Is it on a dead leg or a parallel train? A tap a few metres away can be hydraulically far away. **Time.** A display time is not a sample time. Water takes time to travel from the process point through the sample line, and instruments respond with a lag. Clock offsets add more. **Method.** Free and total chlorine are different analytes. A total value is not a substitute for a free value. Sample temperature, chlorine demand in the container and the delay before reading all shift a result. For turbidity, EPA 815-B-19-010 describes common turbidimeter setups, the SCADA systems that record them and best practices for data quality. It is technical guidance, not binding law for your system. **Quality status.** Was the instrument in verification, calibration, maintenance or out of service? Was the signal frozen, clamped or mis-scaled? A maintenance flag raises a question about reliability. It does not prove the process was safe or unsafe. ### Worked example: alignment of a grab and an online reading All values are supplied case assumptions for a fictional plant. The grab is taken at the clearwell inlet at 08:14. The analyzer is fed from the clearwell outlet. The contact-zone travel time is a supplied input of 31.9 min. How that basis is derived is taught in ceu-water-treatment-process-control. The sample line is 24 m of 6.35 mm internal diameter tubing at 400 mL/min, and the analyzer lag is 90 s. Step 1. Line volume: 0.7854 × (0.00635 m)² × 24 m = 7.60 × 10⁻⁴ m³ = 760 mL. Step 2. Line transit: 760 mL ÷ 400 mL/min = 1.90 min. Step 3. Lag: 90 s = 1.50 min. Step 4. Earliest influence on the display: 08:14 + 31.9 + 1.90 + 1.50 min = 08:14 + 35.3 min = 08:49. **Answer:** the 08:14 grab aligns with analyzer readings from about 08:49 onward, not with the 08:14 display. A grab that reads higher than the 08:14 display proves nothing about analyzer accuracy. To challenge the analyzer, take a grab at its own tap, at stable flow, with the analyte form matched. ### Worked example: bounding an excursion below a target Free chlorine is logged every five minutes against an internal warning of 0.60 mg/L, a target with no legal status. Readings were 0.66 at 08:05, 0.58 at 08:10, 0.55 at 08:15, no data at 08:20, and 0.61 at 08:25 mg/L. Step 1. Observations below 0.60 mg/L: 08:10 and 08:15, so two observations. Step 2. Minimum duration: 08:15 − 08:10 = 5 min. Step 3. Maximum duration: the downward crossing was after 08:05 and the upward crossing was at or before 08:25, so 08:25 − 08:05 = 20 min. **Answer:** report a bound, not a point value. The duration below the target is at least 5 and at most 20 minutes, with one missing interval at 08:20. Do not enter an interpolated value as recorded data. ### Conflicts and the parallel response When records disagree, work the conflict and keep protection running. The weak answer is "we could not determine the cause, so we waited." The stronger answer is "we did not know which record was right, so we kept the more protective reading in force while we resolved it, and we documented both." | Conflict observed | Likely explanations | Evidence to retrieve | What you must not conclude | |---|---|---|---| | Grab higher than online, same minute | Different parcels, location, analyte form, lag | Tap drawing, line length and flow, method | That the analyzer reads low | | Online drops, grab at analyzer tap agrees | A real process change | Dose and flow records, source changes | That it is an instrument fault | | Missing intervals during an excursion | Communication dropout, maintenance | Event log, maintenance log | That the gap held the previous value | | No alarm although data show an excursion | Setpoint change, suppression, scan fault | Alarm configuration history | That no alarm means no excursion | The applicable regulation or permit sets any response and any reporting duty. Do not delay a required report while an investigation continues, and do not treat an internal investigation as a substitute for a report. CT is condition specific (the concept is set out in Crittenden et al., *MWH's Water Treatment: Principles and Design*, 3rd ed., Wiley, 2012, disinfection chapters), and its calculation is taught in ceu-water-treatment-process-control and ceu-coagulation-filtration. Here it is enough to know that a CT figure must be tied to its configuration evidence before it supports any conclusion. ### Common errors - **Filling a data gap with the previous value.** A historian that holds the last good value during a communication failure produces a flat line that looks like data. - **Using a total chlorine grab to overturn a free chlorine reading.** Match the analyte form, or do not compare. - **Treating a post-event calibration as retroactive proof.** A check at 11:00 describes performance at 11:00. - **Reporting an internal warning as an exceedance, or the reverse.** - **Comparing same-minute values across a hydraulic lag.** ### Verify before you act Before drawing a conclusion, open the document that supports it: the permit or licence conditions for the parameter and point; the facility procedures for verification, calibration and out-of-range response; the sampling plan; the applicable reporting provisions (for example 40 CFR Part 141 and state rules, or, for the Ontario example, section 18 of the Safe Drinking Water Act, 2002); the instrument manual for response time and failure behaviour; and the SCADA alarm configuration and maintenance history for every point you rely on. Retain the raw data with gaps shown as gaps, the verification record with its standards, and your bounding calculation with its labelled assumptions.
modules.evidence:
### Fictional worked scenario: Brant Hollow Water Treatment Plant

All facility details, operators, records and readings below are fictional and are used only for training. No value here is an authorized limit for any real facility.

**Supplied values.** Online free chlorine analyzer at the treated water sampling point, logged every five minutes. The fictional internal warning is 0.60 mg/L free chlorine, recorded in the plant's limit register as a target with no legal status. Readings for 5 March: 09:00 at 0.81, 09:05 at 0.69, 09:10 at 0.57, 09:15 at 0.54, 09:20 no data, 09:25 no data, 09:30 at 0.63 and 09:35 at 0.79 mg/L.

**Records supplied by the outgoing shift.**

1. A field sheet reading "Cl2 1.04, 09:18, OK" with no location, no free or total designation and no instrument identified.
2. A logbook entry stating "residual below target for exactly 10 minutes, verified by grab, no further action."
3. An analyzer calibration certificate dated 5 March at 14:40, noting "instrument confirmed accurate, data for the day valid."

**Records to reject or qualify.** Entry 2 states an exact duration the data cannot support, and it cites a grab with no location or analyte form, so the grab cannot overturn an online free chlorine reading. Entry 3 is an unsupported retroactive claim: a 14:40 calibration describes 14:40, not 09:10. Keep it as a separate fact with its own timestamp.

**Worked solution.** Observations below 0.60 mg/L: 09:10 at 0.57 and 09:15 at 0.54, so two observations. Minimum duration = 09:15 − 09:10 = 5 min. Maximum duration = 09:30 − 09:05 = 25 min, because the downward crossing is after 09:05 and the upward crossing is at or before 09:30 with 09:20 and 09:25 missing.

**Defensible statement for handover.** Free chlorine fell below the fictional internal warning on two recorded intervals. The excursion is bounded between 5 and 25 minutes, with two missing intervals at 09:20 and 09:25. The 09:18 field value is set aside pending its location and analyte form. Whether any reporting duty arises is decided by the applicable regulation or permit, not by the internal target.
modules.assignment: Annotate the time series and identify every unsupported statement in the draft conclusion. Build a comparison checklist for the field value. Write an evidence request covering instrument quality, sample identity and treatment significance. Then write a 150 to 250 word event update with separate facts, hypotheses and unresolved risks. Do not infer a CT requirement or prescribe a chemical setting.
rubric: Identifies the two below-target observations and the missing interval without inventing an exact exposure duration.
Checks field or online location, time, method and maintenance context; does not treat the field value as automatic invalidation.
Keeps the internal target separate from any legal threshold and runs verification and response review in parallel.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Expected criticisms: field location and method unverified, analyzer cause not established, exact duration unsupported, harmlessness and closure unproven. Ask whether the later verification sample settles the earlier reading; it does not. Accept gaps or clearly marked interpolation, but require the original missingness to stay visible. Return any answer that invents a CT threshold, prescribes a dosing change or treats the internal target as a legal limit.

checks.prompt: During a shift review, the SCADA alarm panel shows no active or acknowledged chlorine alarms for the past 12 hours. What can the operator properly conclude from the silent panel alone?
choices: That the treated water met each applicable requirement for the full 12 hour period
That the online analyzer was verified as accurate at some point during the window
Very little, because alarms can be suppressed, out of scan, in maintenance mode or fed by a failed sensor
That no bench confirmation of residual is needed before the operating records are signed for the whole shift
checks.explanation: An alarm proves only that the configured logic was satisfied by the signal that reached it. A silent panel does not prove compliance, because the point may be suppressed, out of scan or fed by a sensor reading a plausible wrong number. The compliance option turns an engineered notification into a legal finding. The verification option invents a calibration record that the panel cannot show. The bench-check option assumes a silent alarm removes a verification step that the procedure may require.

checks.prompt: Which description matches a target as the term is used in the four categories of number?
choices: A written trigger in a facility procedure that starts increased sampling, a source switch or an alarm reset
A condition imposed by regulation or by the system's permit or licence
A configured value with deadband and delay that drives a SCADA notification
An internal operating preference that keeps the process comfortably away from trouble
checks.explanation: A target is an internal operating preference, so missing one is a process question, not a legal one. The procedure option describes an action level, a trigger that starts a response. The permit option describes a requirement, which carries legal or permit status that a target lacks. The SCADA option describes an alarm, an engineered notification with deadband and delay. Confusing these leads operators to report internal misses as exceedances, or to assume that meeting a target discharges a legal duty.

checks.prompt: In a limit register template, the value column is deliberately left as a pointer to the governing document rather than filled in with a number. Why is that the sound approach?
choices: The correct figure is the one in that facility's own approval, procedure or sampling plan
Recording a number in a register would make the register a legal reporting record
Operators are not permitted to keep written copies of numeric comparison values
Numeric values change too often for any controlled document to record them reliably over a single shift
checks.explanation: Two systems can carry different numbers for the same parameter because their permits differ, so the register points to the document that governs the system in front of you. The legal-record option misstates what makes a record a reporting record. The copies option has no basis in the register's design. The volatility option misidentifies the problem, which is source and scope rather than how often a value changes.

checks.prompt: A sample line is 24 m of 6.35 mm internal diameter tubing and carries 400 mL/min. Using these supplied assumptions, what is the transit time through the line?
choices: About 7.60 minutes, from using the diameter as the radius and so quadrupling the area
About 1.90 minutes
About 0.95 minutes, from halving the line length to 12 m
About 0.76 minutes, from reading the line volume in litres as though it were minutes
checks.explanation: The line volume is 0.7854 × (0.00635 m)² × 24 m = 7.60 × 10⁻⁴ m³, or 760 mL. Dividing by the 400 mL/min flow gives 1.90 min. The 7.60 minute option uses the diameter as the radius, which quadruples the area. The 0.95 minute option halves the line length. The 0.76 minute option reports the volume in litres as minutes without dividing by flow.

checks.prompt: An online analyzer at a fictional plant displays free chlorine of 0.62 mg/L. A handheld reading taken at a different tap on a parallel header reports total chlorine of 0.78 mg/L. What is the best interpretation?
choices: The analyzer is reading 0.16 mg/L low and should be recalibrated this shift
The handheld reading is faulty, since total chlorine cannot exceed free chlorine in this water
No analyzer bias is shown, since the analyte forms and the sampling points differ
The difference confirms chlorine demand developing between the two locations
checks.explanation: Free and total chlorine are different analytes, and the two taps draw different water, so the pair cannot judge analyzer bias. The recalibration option treats a method and location mismatch as an instrument error. The handheld option is wrong because total chlorine can exceed free chlorine, for example when combined chlorine is present, so the reading is not itself a fault. The demand option assumes that two different parcels of water can show a demand difference.

checks.prompt: A turbidimeter log shows a maintenance flag covering a two hour block. What does the flag establish about water quality during that block?
choices: That the logged values may be used unchanged once the technician signs the record
That the filtered water was acceptable because the readings were operator supervised
That the filtered water was unacceptable and must be treated as an exceedance
Nothing on its own, since it raises a reliability question rather than answering it
checks.explanation: Quality status tells you how much weight a signal can carry, not what the water was doing. The flag does not prove the process was safe and does not prove it was unsafe. The signature option assumes that a signature validates the values. The supervision option treats presence as evidence. The exceedance option assumes that a reliability flag proves a bad result.

modules.title: Reconstruct sample identity and result history
objectives: Decide which record a result rests on when the sample identifiers disagree.
Distinguish a report amendment from evidence that the original result was invalid.
Document sampling uncertainty without suppressing a result or moving it across a threshold.
modules.lesson: ### A result is a number attached to a sample A reported result is a number attached to a physical object. That object was taken from a particular place at a particular time, moved under particular conditions, and analysed by a particular method. Reconstruction asks whether the number you rely on still belongs to that object. It also asks what the answer means for the decisions you have already made and for the records that repeat the number. The full work of sample identity is a separate skill. Field and laboratory identifier registers, holding-time arithmetic, receipt conditions and duplicate precision are taught in ceu-sampling-data-quality. This module assumes that reconstruction and uses only its outcome: which record the decision may rest on, and what must be corrected. ### Classify the discrepancy before choosing a correction The correction depends on the class of the discrepancy. Four classes cover most cases. - **Traceability.** You cannot be certain which object produced the number. A sample point code that disagrees between records is a traceability problem until an attributable statement from the laboratory or the sampler resolves it. - **Integrity or representativeness.** The object no longer represents the water it was meant to characterise, or it was never the intended water. A holding time that has passed, or a different tap sampled than planned, sits here. The result is qualified, and it is not cured by relabelling. - **Reporting.** The number was correct but was carried wrongly into a summary, a spreadsheet or a notice. Fix the document that carries the error, and leave the laboratory record alone. - **Invalidation.** The laboratory finds that its own value was never valid, usually because of a calculation, dilution or transcription error, and reissues a different value. The original was never reliable. The history stays on file. | Observation | Classification | Does an amended report resolve it? | Effect on the original result | Effect on the reporting record | |---|---|---|---|---| | Point code differs only on the laboratory report; bottle ID agrees | Traceability | Yes, with an attributable laboratory statement | Stands unchanged | Both versions kept; notice history unchanged | | Sampler confirms a different tap was sampled | Representativeness | No | Valid for the tap actually sampled | May change which plan obligation was met | | Laboratory's own calculation error, value reissued | Invalidation | The reissue replaces the value but does not erase history | The original value was never valid | A new knowledge date starts for the corrected value | | Summary spreadsheet differs from the laboratory report | Reporting | No; correct the summary | Laboratory result unchanged | Check whether any notice relied on the wrong figure | | Holding time exceeded before analysis | Integrity | No | Qualified; a non-detect is weak evidence | Reporting duties still apply to the result as reported | A qualified result is not a deleted result. The qualification is recorded beside the number, so a reviewer can see both the number and its limitation. ### Keep two timelines Every reconstruction answers two questions. What was true about the water? What did the system know, and when? An amendment that changes a location code does not restart the clock on anything. An amendment that replaces an invalid value creates a new knowledge date for the corrected value. The original receipt date still documents what the operator in charge reasonably knew and acted on at that time. Overwriting the first value removes the second timeline altogether. ### Worked example: recomputing an annual average after a reissue The figures are fictional. Trihalomethane results, in micrograms per litre, were reported for four quarters: Q3 2023 at 108.2, Q4 2023 at 96.4, Q1 2024 at 88.1 and Q2 2024 at 92.3. The Q2 2024 value was reissued on 3 July 2024 as 131.6, after the laboratory found that a dilution factor had been applied incorrectly. Step 1. Original running average at the end of Q2 2024: (108.2 + 96.4 + 88.1 + 92.3) ÷ 4 = 385.0 ÷ 4 = 96.25 µg/L. Step 2. Recomputed average with the reissued value: (108.2 + 96.4 + 88.1 + 131.6) ÷ 4 = 424.3 ÷ 4 = 106.075 µg/L, or about 106.1 µg/L. Step 3. Change caused by the reissue: 106.075 − 96.25 = 9.825 µg/L. **Answer:** the reissue moves the running average from 96.25 to about 106.1 µg/L. Recompute every averaging period that the amended value enters, not only the current one. Keep both averages, both source values and both dates. Any notice or public statement that used 96.25 needs a dated correction. Do not overwrite the spreadsheet cell and move on, because the overwritten cell is the evidence a reviewer needs. The averaging basis and any limit are set by the applicable regulation or permit. This example uses neither. ### Document uncertainty without suppressing the result Every result carries uncertainty. Reporting it honestly is different from arguing a result away. Suppose a laboratory reports 9.3 µg/L with an expanded uncertainty of ±1.9 µg/L, and the comparison value in use for the example is 10 µg/L. The interval 7.4 to 11.2 µg/L spans the comparison value. You report and act on the reported value, 9.3 µg/L, under the applicable requirement. You do not add or subtract uncertainty to move the number across the threshold. You document that the result sits within measurement uncertainty of the comparison, and you flag it for follow-up sampling under the plan. Precision checks on field duplicates, and the statistics behind them, are taught in ceu-sampling-data-quality. Write the acceptance criterion down before sampling. Choosing a limit after seeing the numbers is not quality control. ### Common errors - **Treating a laboratory amendment as proof the event did not happen.** A location correction leaves the detection, the receipt time and the notification history exactly as they were. - **Backfilling blank cells from memory.** A field sheet with no collection time has a gap. An estimate written in weeks later, as though it were observed, creates a false record. - **Using a quality control failure to delete an inconvenient result.** A failed blank describes its own preparation pathway. Document what the control represents, obtain the laboratory's qualification and keep the result on file. - **Overwriting the summary spreadsheet.** Editing a cell in place destroys the knowledge timeline. Keep each version, date each change and name the person who made it. ### Verify before you act Retrieve and read these documents, in this order: 1. The system's permit or licence, which names the sampling points and monitoring conditions. The sampling point named in the approval governs, not a shorthand used on a tag. 2. The sampling plan or standard operating procedure in force on the collection date. Use the version then, not the current version. 3. The laboratory's method instruction for that test, including holding time and receipt condition, obtained from the laboratory that performed the analysis. 4. The operator designation and duty provisions. Ontario example: sections 23 and 25 to 27 of Ontario Regulation 128/04. 5. The reporting provisions that apply to the result. Examples to start from are 40 CFR Part 141 and state rules in the United States, and, for the Ontario example, section 18 of the Safe Drinking Water Act, 2002 with the adverse drinking water results bulletin. The bulletin states that the duty arises immediately after the adverse result is obtained. Check the current regulation for any timing that applies. 6. Every version of the laboratory report, the transfer and courier records and the receipt record, plus laboratory correspondence attributable to a named person and dated. Reject an unsigned, undated note and document the rejection.
modules.evidence:
### Fictional worked scenario: a clerical correction and an undated note

All facilities, operators, laboratories and records below are fictional and are used only for training. No value here is an authorized limit.

Harrowgate Wells Drinking Water System is a fictional small municipal residential system. An adverse bacteriological result is under review during a handover.

**Supplied records**

1. Field sheet: distribution sample, point coded D-12, bottle B-4417, collected 08:20 on 9 July, sampler J. Okonkwo.
2. Transfer record: bottle B-4417, point D-12, courier pickup at 11:40 on 9 July.
3. Laboratory report version 1, issued 9 July: bottle B-4417, point D-21, E. coli detected. Verbal notice given to the operator in charge at 14:10 on 9 July.
4. Laboratory report version 2, issued 12 July: identical result and receipt time, point code corrected from D-21 to D-12. A signed clarification from the laboratory quality manager states the location code was mistyped at login.
5. Logbook note, undated and unsigned: "Lab says first report was a false positive, original cancelled, no notification needed."
6. Email showing written notice to the required parties sent at 09:25 on 11 July.

**Record to reject.** The logbook note in item 5 is undated, unattributed and contradicted by the laboratory's own signed clarification, which changes only the location code and expressly leaves the result unchanged. No laboratory document withdraws the detection. Reject the note, and document the rejection and its reason. Do not delete it.

**Worked solution.** The detection stands. The amendment is a traceability correction, not an invalidation. The timing of the written notice is a separate question for the applicable regulation, and the classroom assumption of 24 hours after the verbal report gives: from 14:10 on 9 July to 14:10 on 10 July is the window, and the written notice was sent at 09:25 on 11 July. That is 19 h 15 min after the window closed. The 12 July amendment does not reset that clock, because it corrected a location code only.

**Answer.** Retain both report versions, the signed clarification, the field and transfer records, the rejected logbook note and a dated correction memo. Confirm the reporting duties against the applicable regulation, and for the Ontario example section 18 of the Safe Drinking Water Act, 2002.

Identifies an active reporting review and the missing notification evidence without assuming the amendment cancels it.
modules.facilitatorGuide: The second report corrects the point code and leaves the detection unchanged. A passing learner does not declare compliance resolved, or external notices completed, from these documents. Ask what evidence would be required to say a recipient was reached. Use this case to separate the analytical record from the operational response record, and reject any draft that treats the undated note as evidence.

checks.prompt: Three records for one fictional sample, the field sheet, the transfer record and the laboratory report, were all typed by the same operator from memory two weeks after collection. What does their agreement establish?
choices: Little, because the records share one author and are not independent
It resolves any holding time question raised by the laboratory report
It permits the sampling point code on the field sheet to be corrected
It confirms sample identity because the three records match exactly
checks.explanation: Reconciliation draws its strength from records created at different times by different people. Records typed later from one person's memory are a single source, so their agreement adds nothing. The holding-time option asks agreement to answer a question it cannot answer. The correction option treats agreement as attributable evidence. The exact-match option treats matching text as confirmation when the sources are not independent.

checks.prompt: When rebuilding a result history, why does the review start with the field sheet rather than with the laboratory report?
choices: The field sheet establishes the laboratory sample identifier that the laboratory assigns
The laboratory report may inherit earlier errors and may be reissued later
The field sheet is the one record a laboratory cannot amend, so it is always authoritative
Laboratory reports are not part of the sample identity trail at all
checks.explanation: The report sits at the end of the chain. It can carry forward a field or transfer error, and it is the document most likely to be reissued, so the review begins with the earliest independent records. The identifier option reverses who assigns the laboratory identifier. The unamendable option is wrong, because any record can be corrected through an attributable trail. The excluded-report option is wrong because reports are part of the identity trail.

checks.prompt: A transfer record for a fictional sample does not state a receipt temperature. What should the reviewer enter in that cell of the sample identity register?
choices: The field sheet temperature, since transport conditions rarely change
The temperature on the laboratory receipt stamp for that batch
Nothing, because a blank cell is itself information about the record
A typical courier value, so that the register table can be completed
checks.explanation: Blank means the record is silent, and that silence is a finding worth keeping. Copying a value from another record, as in the field sheet and batch options, merges independent sources and hides where the information came from. A typical courier value is invented and destroys the register's traceability.

checks.prompt: A licensed laboratory reported 0.38 mg/L for a fictional sample, and the annual summary spreadsheet shows 0.83 mg/L. How is this discrepancy classified and corrected?
choices: A traceability problem; request a reissued report with a new sample code
A representativeness problem; note that the wrong tap was probably sampled
An integrity problem; the sample must be recollected and reanalysed promptly
A reporting problem; correct the summary and document the correction made
checks.explanation: The laboratory value was correct and was carried wrongly into a summary, which is a reporting problem fixed in the summary with a documented correction. The traceability option mistakes a transcription error for a sample identity error. The representativeness option has no evidence about the tap. The integrity option is wrong because nothing happened to the physical sample, so recollection addresses the wrong defect.

checks.prompt: A laboratory reissues a corrected value on 3 July for a sample first reported on 18 May. What does the original receipt date still document?
choices: What the operator in charge knew and acted on at that time
The corrected concentration, which replaces the original in every record
Nothing, because the reissued report supersedes all earlier dates
The date on which the field sheet was typed up
checks.explanation: A reissue creates a new knowledge date for the corrected value, but the original receipt still shows what was known and acted on at the time. The corrected-concentration option treats a reissue as overwriting history. The superseded option erases the knowledge timeline. The field-sheet option confuses the receipt of a laboratory report with the typing of a field sheet.

checks.prompt: A licensed laboratory finds an internal dilution calculation error, withdraws its first reported value for a fictional sample and issues a different number. What has the laboratory done?
choices: Confirmed the original value and added an uncertainty qualifier to it
Stated that the original reported value should not have been relied upon
Relabelled the same result under a corrected sampling point code alone, with no other change
Cured a field holding time exceedance by reissuing the report version
checks.explanation: An internal calculation error means the first number was never valid, so this is invalidation rather than relabelling. The qualifier option keeps the original as valid. The relabelling option changes a code and leaves the number intact. The holding-time option assumes a reissue can cure a defect in the physical sample, which it cannot.

modules.title: Manage reporting, corrective action and closure as separate tasks
objectives: Distinguish internal escalation from applicable external reporting.
Build a communication record that shows attempts, contacts and directions.
Specify evidence-based closure criteria and accountable follow-up.
modules.lesson: ### Separate the event into accountable tasks This is study and training material, not operating or compliance instruction. The pilot is non-credit. Facilities, operators, records and timestamps are fictional. Numerical inputs are supplied case assumptions for teaching. Reporting requirements are set by the applicable regulation or permit and are identified separately from those assumptions. An adverse drinking-water event creates several responsibilities that progress at different speeds. Internal escalation brings supervision into the response. External reporting meets applicable legal duties. Protective action addresses the condition. Verification shows whether the action worked. Closure records what is complete, what supports that, and what remains open. Do not let one task stand in for another. A supervisor's acknowledgement does not show that an external report occurred. An incident reference does not show that corrective action was carried out. A later acceptable result does not, by itself, resolve the event. Give each task its own status, such as not started, attempted, acknowledged, awaiting evidence or complete, with an evidence reference and an accountable person. ### Establish the reporting basis before interpreting progress Find the reporting provisions first. The applicable regulation or permit sets the trigger, the timing, the recipients and the channel. Examples to start from are 40 CFR Part 141 and state rules in the United States, and the provincial or territorial regulation in Canada. For the Ontario example, section 18 of the Safe Drinking Water Act, 2002 establishes the duty, and the Ontario bulletin points to section 16-3 of Schedule 16 to Ontario Regulation 170/03. The bulletin states that the duty arises immediately after the adverse result is obtained. A bulletin supports interpretation but does not replace the legal text. Check the current regulation before relying on any timing. Establish who received the result, when, what it concerned, and which duties apply to each party. A laboratory's communication may be important evidence, but it must not be assumed to discharge the duties of an owner or operating authority. Internal review should support accurate communication without becoming an approval barrier. A result does not become reportable only when a manager agrees it is serious. A shift roster identifies who is present. It does not establish who holds a designated responsibility. For the Ontario example, sections 23 and 25 to 27 of Ontario Regulation 128/04 set designation and duties. If a result is disputed, separate the reporting question from the investigation question. An unsupported belief that a sample was contaminated is not evidence that the original record can be discarded. Keep the original result, the clarification request and any amendment as distinct records. ### Build a communication record that survives handover A communication log should let another operator reconstruct what was known, what was communicated and what direction followed. Record the event identifier, the time, the recipient, the channel, the person reached, the information supplied, any acknowledgement, the reference and the outstanding follow-up. State the time zone, and distinguish event time from entry time. | Record element | Evidence to enter | Judgment it supports | |---|---|---| | Trigger and receipt | Result identifier, receipt time, recipient | What started the response | | Internal escalation | Person contacted, attempt time, acknowledgement | Attempts versus confirmed awareness | | External reporting | Required recipient, channel, person reached, time, contents | Whether the applicable pathway was completed | | Directions | Issuer, exact wording, time, scope, any clarification | What follow-up was required | | Verification | Method, location, record, acceptance basis | Whether the action achieved its result | | Outstanding work | Named owner, dependency, next review point | Prevents an open task from disappearing | An unanswered call is an attempt. A voicemail is evidence of a message left, not of receipt by the required recipient. A call-duration entry corroborates contact but cannot show what was said. Do not paraphrase a conditional direction into an unconditional approval. A late entry must remain recognisable as late, and it must show both times and its basis. ### Worked example: timing without declaring compliance **Classroom assumption, for arithmetic only and not a rule:** written notice is due within 24 hours after the verbal report. The applicable regulation or permit sets the real interval. The fictional Cedar Inlet system received a reportable adverse result at 09:00 on 12 May 2026. A supervisor acknowledged it at 09:01. Verbal reports were completed at 09:03. Written notice was submitted at 08:40 on 13 May, with a retained confirmation. Step 1. Internal acknowledgement: 09:01 − 09:00 = 1 min. This is awareness, not reporting. Step 2. Verbal reporting from receipt: 09:03 − 09:00 = 3 min. Step 3. Verbal report to midnight: 24 h 00 min − 9 h 03 min = 14 h 57 min. Step 4. Midnight to written submission: 8 h 40 min. Step 5. Total elapsed: 14 h 57 min + 8 h 40 min = 23 h 37 min, which leaves a 23-minute margin. **Answer:** on the classroom assumption, the timing element is supported, subject to confirming the recipients, the content and the submission evidence. The 3-minute gap does not set an acceptable delay for immediate reporting, and the acknowledgement does not start the written-notice clock. If a draft existed at 08:40 but was not submitted, the calculation shows preparation, not reporting. ### Worked example: water volume passing a measurement point The validated flow record gives 36 L/s from 14:12 to 14:20, and 24 L/s from 14:20 to 14:30. The measurement point is the outlet under investigation, and the clocks are synchronised. This calculation supports investigation planning. It does not decide whether reporting is required. Step 1. First interval: 480 s × 36 L/s = 17,280 L. Step 2. Second interval: 600 s × 24 L/s = 14,400 L. Step 3. Total: 31,680 L = 31.68 m³. **Answer:** 31.68 m³ passed the measurement point. A simple average of 36 and 24 L/s (30 L/s over 18 minutes) gives 32,400 L, which overstates the volume by 0.72 m³. The simple average gives equal weight to unequal durations, so reject it. The calculated volume is not automatically customer exposure, because storage and routing affect where the water went. ### Define closure before the reassuring evidence arrives Closure needs explicit criteria, drawn from the applicable requirements, any direction from the authority, the facility response procedure and the event's verification needs. Keep reporting completion, operational verification and event closure distinct. Reporting may be complete while verification is pending. A repair may be finished while the cause is still uncertain. "Instrument serviced" records maintenance, not valid readings. "Sample collected" records collection, not an outcome. A later reading inside a target describes a later condition. It does not reconstruct the earlier interval. Compare the evidence with criteria set in advance, not with criteria the evidence happens to satisfy. Assign every unresolved item to a named person, with a next review point from the governing procedure. ### Common errors - **Calling the supervisor and marking external reporting complete.** Internal escalation and statutory reporting are different tasks. - **Treating a sent draft as a submitted notice.** - **Using one acceptable reading to close the event.** - **Replacing original records with corrected summaries.** - **Applying a sample result to the wrong location.** ### Verify before you act Consult the current reporting provisions that apply to your system, including the trigger, any exemption, the recipients and the channels. For the Ontario example, that means section 18 of the Safe Drinking Water Act, 2002 and the current bulletin. Consult the permit or licence, the adverse-result procedure, the reporting contact list and the validated treatment procedures. Check designation records against the applicable operator provisions. Before recording closure, confirm who has authority to decide, which criteria apply and whether each has evidence. Keep reporting, corrective action and closure visible separately until each has its own support.

### Fictional worked scenario: a timing claim and a rejected note

The facility, operators, records and readings in this scenario are fictional. All timestamps and measurements are supplied case assumptions, not authorized values. The classroom assumption of a 24-hour written-notice window is used only for arithmetic.

At fictional Birch Point Drinking Water System, operator Mira receives a reportable adverse result at 16:10 on 8 June 2026. The communication record supports completion of the immediate verbal reports at 16:14, with recipient names, report contents and acknowledgements retained. Written notice has confirmed submission at 15:50 on 9 June. A supervisor's spreadsheet says, "Reporting clock started with internal acknowledgement at 16:30." Reject that clock basis, because the record does not support it.

**Worked timing solution (classroom assumption):**

- Boundary: 8 June 16:14 + 24 h = 9 June 16:14.
- Time from 16:14 to midnight: 24 h 00 min − 16 h 14 min = 7 h 46 min.
- Elapsed to submission: 7 h 46 min + 15 h 50 min = 23 h 36 min.
- Margin: 24 h 00 min − 23 h 36 min = 0 h 24 min.

**Answer:** the written submission occurred 24 minutes before the boundary. This supports the timing only. It does not show overall event closure, and it is not a general acceptable interval for immediate reporting.

A later turbidity reading of 0.18 NTU comes with a handwritten note, "Clear reading, close event." Reject that conclusion. No applicable acceptance basis accompanies the note, and the directed verification sample remains pending. Report reporting evidence as complete under the supplied assumptions, corrective verification as pending and closure as unsupported. Assign the pending-result review to the incoming designated role, and retain the original note, the rejection rationale and the communication records.
